items: MVCC = Multi-Version Concurrency Control
Readers see a consistent snapshot, never blocking writers
Writers never block readers either — the core Postgres rule
Snapshot isolation ships by default at `READ COMMITTED`
UPDATE writes a NEW row version, marks the old expired
DELETE erases no bytes — it stamps the version expired
Each row version is a `tuple`
A logical row = a chain of tuple versions over time
Consequence 1: rollback is nearly free — no undo replay
Consequence 2: cleanup is not free — VACUUM reclaims later
One trade-off, three symptoms: bloat, autovacuum, wraparound

blocks.title: Terms To Keep
items: dead tuple = invisible to any running or future txn
bloat = dead tuples + unused free space in pages
Bloat lives in table AND index pages

blocks.text: Under 2PL a plain reader takes a shared lock and a writer waits behind it. Postgres avoids that entirely by keeping the old version readable.

blocks.title: One Line
blocks.text: Postgres buys non-blocking reads with garbage it must sweep up later.

items: 23 bytes of header sit before every row's user data
Padded to 24 bytes by alignment
Per-version overhead: header + null bitmap + padding
Every version pays it again — overhead is real
`t_cid` stops a statement from seeing its own output
Newest version's `t_ctid` points at itself
After UPDATE the old one points forward

Assigned lazily — read-only txns get no real xid

blocks.title: Rule Of Thumb
blocks.text: Visible = inserted before your snapshot and not deleted before your snapshot.

Then it re-tests the WHERE clause on that version
That is EvalPlanQual (EPQ)

blocks.title: The Key Insight
blocks.text: The OLDEST snapshot pins every dead tuple newer than it. One idle transaction blocks cleanup database-wide.

items: DELETE only sets xmax — the bytes stay in the page
UPDATE = DELETE + INSERT in one step
The old `t_ctid` redirects to the new version
A concurrent writer walks the chain forward
It lands on the latest version, then re-tests its predicate
Every UPDATE rewrites the ENTIRE row
Flipping one boolean on a 2 KB row costs a 2 KB rewrite
Non-HOT UPDATE inserts into EVERY index on the table
Even indexes on columns you never touched

blocks.title: Write Amplification
blocks.text: A table with 6 indexes turns one UPDATE into 1 heap write plus 6 index writes.

items: Values over ~2 KB move to a side table
Unchanged TOASTed column: the new version reuses the pointer
So a huge text field is not re-written every time
An UPDATE-only table still grows — new versions need room
`fillfactor` defaults to 100 for tables
Lower to 80-90 to reserve in-page room for versions
Deleted rows vanish at commit; space returns only after VACUUM

lines: VACUUM FULL t;  -- rewrite so old pages get the reserve

items: HOT = an UPDATE that touches no index at all
Condition 1: no INDEXED column changed
Condition 2: the new version fits on the SAME page
Both must hold, every time
The old line pointer becomes a redirect
The new tuple gets no index entry at all
Index scans land on the old pointer, follow the chain in-page
HOT chains never cross pages

blocks.title: Why fillfactor Matters
blocks.text: No free room on the page means no HOT. That is the whole reason update-heavy tables want `fillfactor` 80-90.

items: Any page access can trigger `heap_page_prune`
Dead HOT chain members collapse into free space
Cheap and local — no VACUUM needed
But it cannot remove index entries
`PageIsFull` hint tells backends a page is worth pruning
Ratio near 0 on a churning table = a real problem
Cause A: `fillfactor` too high
Cause B: an indexed column keeps changing
Indexing `last_seen_at` or a status counter kills HOT
It kills it for the WHOLE table, not just that column
Fix: move the churning column to a narrow, unindexed table
PG16+ keeps HOT when only a BRIN summarizing index covers the change

blocks.title: Two Benefits, One Cost
items: Benefit: no index write amplification
Benefit: pruning reclaims space without VACUUM
Cost: low fillfactor = more pages, slower seq scans
Its xmax is committed
AND it is older than every active snapshot's xmin horizon
Until then it must stay — someone can still see it
Mark dead tuple space reusable inside the file
Remove the matching entries from every index
Update the visibility map
Exception: VACUUM truncates wholly-empty trailing pages
That truncation grabs a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
VACUUM FULL blocks all reads and writes
`pg_repack` / `pg_squeeze` compact online instead
Free Space Map (`fsm`): per-page free space, so INSERTs reuse room
Visibility Map (`vm`): 2 bits per page — all-visible, all-frozen
all-visible pages enable INDEX ONLY SCANs
The executor then skips the heap fetch entirely
`maintenance_work_mem` sizes the dead-tid array
Too small = repeated index passes over the same table
PG17 replaced the array with a TID store
Far less memory, far fewer repeat index scans

blocks.title: Reusable ≠ Returned
blocks.text: Plain VACUUM never shrinks the file. It only stops it from growing further.

items: Launcher wakes every `autovacuum_naptime` (default 60s)
It starts workers per database
`autovacuum_max_workers` defaults to 3
3 workers across hundreds of tables is a common bottleneck

caption.text: Your UPDATE didn't change that row — it wrote a whole new copy and left the old one on disk. That one design choice explains free rollbacks, table bloat, autovacuum, and the 4.2-billion transaction cliff, all at once. 10 pages on tuple headers, snapshots, HOT updates, and the monitoring queries that catch a frozen horizon before it stops your writes.
